decision_context: The Triangle Shirtwaist Company operates a large garment factory on the upper floors of a New York building. The workforce is predominantly young immigrant women working among large quantities of cloth, paper patterns and other combustible material. Management has legitimate concerns about theft, unauthorised departures and production control. An inspection account describes exit doors with locks that were unlocked during the visit. Routine door status, individual knowledge and the completeness of fire protection remain uncertain. The question is how management should balance property/production controls against emergency escape and fire risk before any catastrophic fire is assumed.
decision_question: Should the factory maintain access-control and low-cost fire-safety arrangements that can obstruct or narrow emergency escape, or redesign security and production controls so all workers have rapid unobstructed emergency egress and stronger fire protections?
actors: Triangle Shirtwaist Company owners and managers
building/factory supervisors responsible for access and safety
available_actions: Maintain current access-control practices, including locking or tightly controlling selected exits during work to prevent theft/unauthorised departure, while relying on existing stairs, elevators, fire escape and basic firefighting equipment.
Keep every required emergency exit unlocked and readily openable from inside during occupancy, using guards, checks or other less dangerous methods for theft/attendance control.
Add regular fire drills, clearly marked escape routes and management responsibility for verifying exits remain usable throughout every shift.
Install stronger active/passive fire protection such as sprinklers, improved alarms/hoses and better compartmentation where technically feasible.
Reduce overcrowding/combustible accumulation and review whether the external fire escape and stair capacity can safely evacuate the workforce.

affected_parties.party: Factory workers, predominantly young immigrant women
affected_parties.known_interests_or_risks: Life, bodily safety, ability to evacuate, income, bargaining power and freedom from being trapped by workplace control systems during emergency.
Property protection, production continuity, labour discipline, cost of safety improvements and legal/business responsibility.
Loss of income, caregiving and family members if workers are killed or injured.

affected_parties.party: Other building occupants, firefighters and surrounding public
affected_parties.known_interests_or_risks: Fire spread, rescue burden and safety during a high-rise industrial fire.
Enforcing fire/building rules, public trust and responsibility for known high-rise factory hazards.

known_evidence.claim: The factory occupies upper floors and employs a large workforce in rooms containing substantial combustible cloth, paper patterns and garment-production material.
Fire in such a high-rise factory can develop quickly and makes evacuation capacity/time a life-critical safety factor.

Theft and unauthorised departure are management concerns. Guards or checks that leave emergency exits openable are proposed alternatives; their effectiveness and cost have not been established for this factory.

An inspector reports that stairway exit doors had locks but were unlocked when inspected during work. This observation does not establish routine locking practices, the status of every exit on other shifts, or what any particular manager knew.
The supplied account identifies fire pails and a hose among the factory protections. It does not establish a complete installation inventory or routine readiness of this equipment.
An external fire escape and a limited number of stairs/elevators provide evacuation routes, but failure/obstruction of one route can substantially reduce available capacity for a large workforce.
Workers are economically dependent on employment and individually have limited practical power to redesign exits, install sprinklers or override management security rules.

Keeping exits openable and using non-blocking security controls are physically distinct measures. Whether particular guards or checks would meet security needs at an acceptable cost remains uncertain.

Fire drills, unobstructed exits and stronger fire protection impose financial/operational costs, but those costs are borne primarily by the firm while catastrophic injury/death risk from inadequate precautions falls primarily on workers.

known_uncertainties: The exact probability and timing of a serious factory fire.
The cost and technical feasibility of every proposed sprinkler/building modification in the existing building.
The precise day-to-day door-locking practice and who authorises or knows each exit's status during every shift.
How effectively guards/checks could control theft without obstructing evacuation.
Whether existing building/fire rules legally require every proposed improvement; moral adequacy is not identical to minimum legal compliance.

Whether automatic sprinkler protection is installed; the supplied installation evidence does not settle this. The selected action describes a locking/control policy whose routine operation is not established by the single inspection.
known_alternatives: Unlocked outward/openable emergency egress combined with non-blocking theft/attendance controls.
Fire drills, exit checks and named supervisory responsibility at the start and during each shift.
Incremental sprinkler/alarm/escape improvements prioritised by life-safety value where full retrofit cannot occur immediately.
Reduce combustible accumulation/crowding and verify escape-route capacity.
Independent fire-safety inspection with corrective-action deadlines rather than relying only on internal management judgement.
requested_output: Separate the legitimate objective of theft/attendance control from the chosen means of controlling exits.
Assess whether cost/productivity/property benefits are being obtained by exporting disproportionate safety risk to low-power workers.
Do not assume that continued employment equals meaningful consent to avoidable lethal hazards.
Compare less dangerous alternatives that achieve the same legitimate business purpose.
Assess duties of both employer and public inspector/authority without inventing criminal intent.
Give a Moral Code assessment using only the pre-fire risk structure, not the later death toll.
